title: First Mass, or first in years
hookLine: the hardest part is walking through the door; nobody at the door asks where you've been
last: SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.

lines: THE HARDEST PART IS THE DOOR.
cards: A church parking lot, ten minutes before Sunday Mass. Someone sits in a car with the engine off, watching families cross the lot. They haven't been inside in eleven years.
Or they've never been inside at all, and a friend said, just come once. Their hands are a little sweaty. What if everyone can tell?
What if I stand up at the wrong time? People who've made that walk say it afterward: the hardest part was the door.

teach.b: Parish comes from a Greek word, paroikia, for people living away from home: neighbors who are also, in a sense, strangers. The first letter of Peter calls Christians, in the Douay-Rheims, "strangers and pilgrims."

So a parish was never a club for people who already belong. It's a house full of people on the way. People walk in for a funeral or a wedding, after a hard year, for a partner, or out of plain curiosity.
And people step away for all kinds of reasons: some stopped believing, some were hurt, some drifted, or were never really taught. Nobody at the door asks which. You're not behind.
What happens inside? Sit anywhere; the back is fine. There's usually a book or a card in the pew with the words.
Stand, sit and kneel when the people around you do. Nobody is grading. At Communion, Catholics who are ready go up to receive.

teach.h: MANY REASONS TO LEAVE, AND TO COME.
teach.b: Anyone who isn't, a guest, someone on the way to becoming Catholic, a Catholic who isn't ready yet, can stay in the pew, or in many parishes come up with arms crossed over the chest for a blessing.
When you want a next step, someone coming back can talk to a priest, and go to confession when they're ready; that's a whole lesson later on.

Adults who want to become Catholic go through a process many parishes now call OCIA, the Order of Christian Initiation of Adults; it used to be called RCIA. Some lifelong Catholics sit in on it as a refresher.
And the line people hear over and over, from the pew next to them, is two words: welcome home.

how: Anyone may attend Mass. Visitors and returning Catholics sit where they like and follow the people around them; those not receiving Communion stay in the pew or, in many parishes, come forward with arms crossed for a blessing. Adults who wish to become Catholic join their parish's OCIA (formerly RCIA).

o: a private club for families who already belong
a cathedral, where a bishop has his seat
people far from home, gathered as a local church

games.q: your first Mass back — tap the pairs.
p: from a Greek word for people far from home
the words, so you can follow

s: you have to know all the responses before you can go to Mass
there's usually a book or card in the pew, and you stand, sit and kneel with the people around you.
you have to go to confession before you're allowed through the door
the door is open to anyone. confession comes before receiving Communion if there's serious sin, not before walking in.
in many parishes, someone not receiving can come up with arms crossed for a blessing
or stay in the pew. both are completely normal.

games.q: Communion time. you're a guest, or a Catholic who isn't ready to receive yet. your whole row stands up. what do you do?
o: go up and receive, so nobody notices.
stay seated, or go up with arms crossed for a blessing.
games.why: either one is completely normal. people let others past all the time, and in many parishes the blessing line is just part of the line.

practice: Picture a church you know, or one you've driven past: your hand on the door handle, the small hush as it closes behind you, a seat near the back. Notice the light and the quiet; nobody turns around.
Sit there a while and let it be all right that you came, and if you pray, say so, in a word or two.

wordCard.voice: Parish. From the Greek for people living away from home: the local church, open to whoever walks in.

orig.note: Greek: a sojourning, living as a neighbor away from home. Through Latin parochia it became parish.

carryVoice: Your line: welcome home. Whether it's your first Mass or your first in years, that's what the door is for. Tomorrow, the water just inside it.
